raw_case_text:
A 56-year-old female came in outpatient with chief complaints of low back pain radiating to both but-tocks, burning sensations to both lower limbs. She had a claudication distance of <100 m. She also complained of weakness in both feet and difficulty to put footwear. Her back VAS was 7 and leg VAS was 8. Her ODI was 74. She gave a history of constitutional symptoms such as loss of weight and appetite. Trial of conservative management was given at multiple hospitals.
Clinical examination revealed bilateral SLR test positive at 30 . Her neurological examination showed grade 3 weakness in both toe and ankle dorsiflexors. Sensations across the bilateral L4 and L5 derma-tomes were reduced by 50%.
Her white blood cell count was 11,000, ESR was 10, and CRP was 45. Radiologically, lumbar spine X-ray (Fig. 1) revealed pars discal osteopenia with decreased disc space between L5 and S1.
Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) (Fig. 2) revealed signal intensity changes suggestive of patchy marrow edema present over the L2 to S1 vertebra up to the upper two-third of the sacral ala, mid por-tion of sacrum, and right iliac bone with associated epidural, pre- and paravertebral soft-tissue exten-sion along bilateral psoas muscles suggestive of infective etiology rather than neoplastic.
While a nuclear positron emission tomography (PET) scan (Fig. 3) showed an increase in radiotracer concentration involving L2-L5 vertebra, S1 vertebra, right Sacroiliac region, and right ilium, which favored a metastatic etiology rather than infection, leading to a diagnostic dilemma.
In view of persistent neurological deficit, pain, a team discussion with oncologists, infectious disease specialists, and orthopedic spine team, Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) (Fig. 2) revealed signal the final decision was made to do a surgical decompression and biopsy from the affected areas. Surgery was performed in the form of laminectomy and decompression by posterior approach and tissue was collected from the right sacral ala. As the pre-operative and intraoperative findings did not favor instability, no instrumented fusion was planned. Histopathological report showed negative metastasis. Microbiology was negative. The patient improved during post-operative period in terms of pain and mobility. VAS scores improved to 4. After 3 months' post-surgery, the patient came back to the clinic with chief complaints of burning sensations in legs and inability to walk and stand for long with discharging sinuses over the back with the similar neurologi-cal profile.
X-ray (Fig. 4) revealed diffuse osteopenia with patchy sclerosis and degenerative changes with lami-nectomy defects.
Contrast MRI (Fig. 5, 6, 7) showed patchy areas of marrow signal abnormality L1, L2, L4, and L5 vertebra and adjoining endplates of L5, S1, and S2 segments. Ring enhancing lesions at L2, L3 levels. Enhancing hyperintense signals in posterior paraspinal muscles at L1-L2. Tiny enhancing lesions on the right ilium. PET scan (Fig. 8, 9, 10) shows lytic areas over L2 to L5 vertebrae and sacral ala and ilium possibility of infective etiology more likely atypical Kochs/brucella/Fungal or any unusual bacterial infection. A progressively increasing in ESR and CRP directed toward an infective etiology. Tests for brucellosis were negative.
The patient underwent repeat surgery in the form of revision decompression. Intraoperatively, there was a thick and hard epidural tissue engulfing the cord and the nerve roots. This unhealthy granulation tissue was carefully removed and sent for analysis. Histopathology (Fig. 11, 12) revealed clumps of basophilic filamentous bacteria in a vaguely rosette-like configuration surrounded by acute inflam-matory cells, characteristic of actinomycosis.
The patient was started on intravenous penicillin G for 4 weeks and followed by oral penicillin for 2 weeks. Wound completely healed by primary intention by 2 weeks. The patient ambulated unassisted with back VAS of 2. Leg VAS reduced to 1.
After 6 weeks, ODI was 16, X Rays (Fig. 13) showed reduced osteopenia, and MRI showed a signifi-cant reduction in marrow signal abnormalities in lumbar and sacral areas (Fig. 14, 15, 16).
At 6 months, we reviewed the patient again. He had complaints of back pain, but the examination did not reveal any positive findings.
At 12 months, the patient was asymptomatic.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 56-year-old female presented with chronic low back pain radiating to both buttocks, bilateral lower limb burning paresthesias, neurogenic claudication (<100 m), and bilateral foot drop/weakness, followed 3 months post-laminectomy by discharging lumbar sinuses.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 56-year-old woman presented with severe low back pain (VAS 7) radiating to both buttocks and burning bilateral lower extremity pain (VAS 8, ODI 74), severe neurogenic claudication (<100 m), bilateral foot/ankle dorsiflexion weakness, anorexia, and weight loss refractory to conservative therapy. Three months after initial posterior L2-S1 laminectomy and sacral ala biopsy (which was nondiagnostic), she returned with recurrent burning leg pain, inability to stand or walk, and discharging sinuses over the lumbar surgical scar.
subjective.past_medical_history: Failed multiple prior conservative treatments; underwent initial posterior lumbar laminectomy and decompression 3 months prior to recurrence.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for severe low back and gluteal pain, burning leg paresthesias, bilateral foot weakness, claudication (<100 m), anorexia, weight loss, and subsequent discharging dorsal sinuses.

objective.physical_examination: Bilateral straight leg raise (SLR) test positive at 30 degrees; grade 3/5 motor weakness in bilateral ankle and great toe dorsiflexors; 50% sensory reduction across bilateral L4 and L5 dermatomes; at 3-month recurrence, discharging sinus tracts were present over the lumbar spine.
objective.routine_investigations: Initial labs: WBC 11,000/mm3, ESR 10 mm/h, CRP 45 mg/L (with progressively rising ESR and CRP at 3-month recurrence). Brucellosis serologic tests were negative. Lumbar spine X-rays showed pars interarticularis/discal osteopenia, narrowed L5-S1 disc space, and subsequent patchy sclerosis with laminectomy defects.
objective.advanced_workup: Initial lumbosacral MRI showed patchy marrow edema from L2 to S1, upper two-thirds of the sacral ala, mid-sacrum, and right ilium with epidural, prevertebral, and bilateral psoas paravertebral soft-tissue extension; 3-month repeat contrast MRI showed patchy marrow signal abnormality in L1-S2, ring-enhancing lesions at L2-L3, posterior paraspinal muscle enhancement at L1-L2, and tiny right iliac lesions. Initial and 3-month FDG-PET/CT scans showed hypermetabolic lytic lesions across L2-S1, right sacroiliac joint, and right ilium. While initial sacral ala biopsy was negative for malignancy and microorganisms, repeat revision decompression biopsy of thick, woody epidural granulation tissue engulfing the thecal sac and nerve roots revealed basophilic filamentous bacterial aggregates in a rosette-like configuration (Splendore-Hoeppli phenomenon/sulfur granules) surrounded by acute inflammatory cells, diagnostic of spinal actinomycosis.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Revision epidural granulation tissue histopathology demonstrating rosette-like basophilic filamentous bacterial clumps (with metastasis and brucellosis excluded) confirmed lumbosacral and pelvic spinal actinomycosis with epidural compression. Treated with revision surgical decompression followed by 4 weeks of IV crystalline penicillin G and 2 weeks of oral penicillin. The sinus tracts healed within 2 weeks, back and leg VAS scores dropped to 2 and 1 (ODI 16) with MRI resolution at 6 weeks, and the patient was completely asymptomatic at 12-month follow-up.
